content.text:
No, it won't. Running `/login` here only changes the team slot, and your personal work keeps its own login.

- **Separate files.** This session saves its login to `~/.claude-company/.credentials.json`. Personal sessions use `~/.claude/.credentials.json`. They're two separate files, not linked or hardlinked, and they already hold different tokens.
- **Nothing copies between them.** No script in `~/.local/bin`, your zsh files, cron or systemd writes to either file. `claude-usage-weeks` only reads the account name.
- **The account is picked by folder.** The `chpwd` rule in `~/.zshrc` (lines 35–41) sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-company` only inside `discourse-graph` and `dg-team-mcp`, and clears it everywhere else. `workday` does the same for the windows it opens. So Claude started anywhere else uses `~/.claude` and stays on your personal account.

The account is fixed when a session starts. A personal session already running won't change, and new sessions follow whichever folder they start in.

Run `/login` here, pick the team account, and I'll check that `~/.claude-company` has switched while `~/.claude` is still on your personal account.

=================== README.md
# Discourse Graphs Review Lab

> **Alpha. LLM-created. Not yet tested in real team use.** This project attempts
> to accurately represent the current workflow used to review Discourse
> Graphs PRs. That workflow is constantly in flux. This package is an evolving
> draft, not an established team process or a guarantee of review correctness.

Automated synthetic checks have been run. They are recorded separately in
[Testing](docs/testing.md) and do not establish teammate, macOS or live-provider
acceptance. The alpha status applies even when automated checks pass.

This private repository packages DG PR triage, pinned detailed reviews, changed-head
refreshes and offline HTML. It keeps one shared assessment record and renderer.
Local review progress is separate from GitHub approval. Provider collection is
read-only and limited to the configured repository in the DiscourseGraphs organization.
The example target is `DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph`; DG Roam and Obsidian clients
remain legitimate review surfaces.

## Start with synthetic data

Use Python 3.11+ (`python3` on macOS). No provider access is needed:

```sh
python scripts/team_review.py sample
```

Open `local/synthetic/index.html`. The example is synthetic DG-shaped data, not a
real PR snapshot. Read [TEAM-INSTALL.md](TEAM-INSTALL.md) for configuration,
authentication, operation, updates and cleanup. The repository source is
`https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/review-lab`.

To preview concrete before/after explanations without provider access:

```sh
python skills/mg-review-lab/scripts/review_lab.py render --input examples/narratives.json --output local/narratives/index.html
```

Open `local/narratives/index.html`, choose either synthetic PR and expand
“The change, explained.” These examples show a published field moving and a
reader's field preference changing, with pseudocode and local diff jumps.

## Use with Codex

Read [mg-review-lab](skills/mg-review-lab/SKILL.md) and supply an explicit local
configuration. The skill routes queue refresh, targeted review, saved prioritization
and HTML rendering. A complete refresh includes fresh evidence and assessment of
every changed/new snapshot. Collection or re-rendering alone is not a code review.

Keep real PR records, source evidence, notes, credentials and local configuration in
ignored `local/` or a private output directory. Do not commit them. Cloning does not
install global skills, profile commands, schedulers or services. No review submission,
comment posting, automated fixes, merging or deployments are included.

## Included

- Configurable reviewer, DG repository, evidence paths and stable localhost port.
- Detached inspection, immutable diff pins and source evidence retained after cleanup.
- Intent/scope assessment, findings/checks, Guided walkthroughs and optional Shape maps.
- Shared offline renderer, local notes/progress and matching-snapshot state transfer.
- Concrete change examples and before/after pseudocode, with legacy narrative support.
- DG-only collector guards and synthetic regression tests.

See [architecture](docs/architecture.md), [portability](docs/portability.md),
[provenance](docs/provenance.md) and [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).
Bundled third-party licenses are retained. No blanket license is granted here.
=================== TEAM-INSTALL.md
# DG alpha installation and operation

Alpha, LLM-created, not yet tested in real team use. This evolving package attempts
to reflect the current DG review workflow, which is constantly in flux.
Canonical DG source: https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/review-lab (private).
Automated synthetic checks are documented separately in docs/testing.md.

## Required tools and access

| Operation | Requirements |
| --- | --- |
| Synthetic rendering, saved HTML, local server | Python 3.11+, browser; standard library only |
| Requested-PR discovery and pinned preparation | Git, authenticated GitHub CLI (`gh`), repository read access |
| Intent assessment | Linear read connector or supplied dated issue/comments/spec evidence |
| DG review prose | Configured target checkout's `.agents/skills/dg-engineering-writing-style/SKILL.md` |
| Optional Shape maps | Node.js 18+, pinned TypeScript 5.5.4; follow `docs/shape.md` |
| Product verification | Target repository instructions and its toolchain; package tests do not replace them |

Credentials stay in GitHub CLI / connector stores. Do not put tokens, raw provider
evidence or local paths in committed configuration. A teammate needs access to the
private canonical repository; granting access or moving ownership requires a team
decision. No account permissions were changed by this draft.

## Install a reviewed source revision

```sh
git clone https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/review-lab.git review-lab
cd review-lab
```

Select the reviewed commit before use. Keep local configuration/data outside tracked
source and export matching notes/progress before updates.

From the cloned source directory, use the following commands. On Windows run `python`; on macOS
run `python3` for every command below. No `npm install` is needed for core rendering.

```sh
python scripts/team_review.py sample
python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'
```

Open `local/synthetic/index.html`. The same shared renderer emits the auxiliary
Archives and Notes pages. This proves rendering without a personal profile function.
It does not exercise provider access or perform a code review.

Copy `team-review.example.json` to `local/team-review.json`. Change all relative
paths so they resolve from that config file's directory. Alternatively use absolute
paths, using forward slashes in JSON on both systems. Set `repository` to a verified DiscourseGraphs repository, `repo_root` to its checkout, and `reviewer` to `authenticated` or a
verified GitHub login. Set disjoint `output_dir` and `temp_root` outside the reviewed
checkout. Set `writing_skill` to the actual DG writing skill. Choose one stable
local server port and browser profile for persistent notes.

```sh
python scripts/team_review.py --config local/team-review.json doctor
gh auth login
python scripts/team_review.py --config local/team-review.json doctor --auth
```

`doctor` is offline by default. `--auth` makes harmless identity/repository reads;
it never logs in or grants scopes. If authentication or connector approval stalls,
report the gap and continue with supplied evidence. No retry loop is defined.

## Codex discovery

For the pilot, tell Codex: “Read `<package>/skills/mg-review-lab/SKILL.md` and
`<package>/skills/mg-review-lab/references/team-setup.md`; use my configuration at
`<config>`.” This needs no global skill installation or personal workflow manager.
All package procedures and supporting skills stay in the canonical repository.

After approval, the maintainer can add a forwarding entry in the team's chosen
discovery collection. It must resolve `REVIEW_LAB_REPO` or an explicit checkout
path, verify the canonical remote and load this repository's skill. Do not install
copied renderer/assets or overwrite an
existing `mg-review-lab` discovery entry. Collision resolution belongs to the owner.

## Queue, review and refresh

1. Collect requested PR metadata with `queue`. This is collection only. It uses
   configured reviewer identity and canonical direct-request / re-request eligibility,
   paginates reviews and timelines, and records exclusions and observation time.
   Search reaching 1,000 results fails with an explicit coverage gap.
2. Ask Codex to triage the eligible PRs from `evidence/queue.json` using the canonical
   queue procedure. Intent, readiness and next action need source evidence. A metadata
   collection is not an assessment or a complete refresh.
3. Prepare selected PRs with `prepare`. The canonical helper creates an isolated
   clone and detached worktrees, verifies GitHub head pins, computes merge bases,
   and discovers competing Linear references. Read its complete manifest.
4. Retrieve full linked intent/comments with pagination. Save dated captures and
   provenance under the run's `context/` or durable evidence directory. Inspect the
   pinned diff and callers; author findings, criteria assessments and exact checks.
   Keep unavailable sources, unrun checks and failed checks visible.
5. Author one shared `lab.json` following `references/record-contract.md`. Use the
   canonical import adapters where useful (`review_lab.py import-review` or
   `import-queue`), then assess the resulting record. Do not pass standalone queue
   schema data directly to the shared renderer. Follow the packaged
   [narrative guide](skills/mg-review-lab/references/narrative.md) for concrete change
   explanations. Newly authored narratives use format version 2; choose a small
   example and before/after rule when they clarify the change. Reauthor older
   narratives from their matching source during a requested review or refresh.
6. Recheck head, base and direct request identity before delivering the current
   review. Changed pins invalidate old findings, passed checks and local completion.
   Refresh requires reassessment of every changed/new snapshot, not just re-rendering.
7. Render and serve the shared record. Export supported notes/progress before
   upgrading or changing origin. Import only state whose snapshot identities match.
8. Run `cleanup` for each prepared manifest in success or failure paths after
   preserving authored records/check logs. It retains pinned diffs, metadata and
   context outside the temporary clone. Dirty inspection worktrees are preserved
   for inspection. Cleanup does not remove durable evidence or rendered HTML.

```sh
python scripts/team_review.py --config local/team-review.json queue
python scripts/team_review.py --config local/team-review.json prepare --pr 123 --linear-ticket 123=ENG-456
python scripts/team_review.py --config local/team-review.json render --input /path/to/lab.json
python scripts/team_review.py --config local/team-review.json serve
python scripts/team_review.py --config local/team-review.json cleanup --manifest /path/to/prepare-manifest.json
```

These commands are documented for future authorized operation. Recorded checks are synthetic/local validation, not real team acceptance. `serve` uses the existing hidden loopback server and
opens no browser. It rejects conflicting servers instead of changing the origin.
Local completion and notes never approve GitHub or change Linear. No provider-write
command, automated fix, comment-resolution loop or scheduler is added.

## Updates and removal

Export local state. Preserve the config, `lab.json`, evidence, archives and browser
origin. Check the canonical checkout is clean; fetch and inspect the proposed next
release commit, then switch explicitly and rerun offline smoke/tests and doctor.
Do not merge unrelated local source changes automatically. Re-render saved data;
this does not fetch providers. Verify overlapping state imports preserve matching
snapshots and invalidate changed heads. File Viewed/theme are outside the supported
state export and remain browser-local, as documented upstream.

Removal: stop only the server started for this package, remove only the owned
forwarding discovery entry if one was installed, and preserve/export private review
data. This draft does not add install, auto-start, update or removal automation.

## Acceptance still required

Record OS/version, Python/Git/gh versions, selected source commit and exact commands
for each pilot. Windows synthetic validation is recorded in the task evidence.
macOS commands are documented but **not validated** on this host.

- Team owner confirms canonical repository access and release/discovery source.
- One Windows teammate and one macOS teammate bootstrap without another contributor's filesystem.
- Each discovers their own requests, triages one PR, opens one pinned detailed review,
  and re-reviews a changed head with visible invalidation.
- Exercise notes/progress export/import, missing Linear, failed check, provider
  authentication failure, clean cleanup and dirty-worktree preservation.
- Confirm no GitHub/Linear state changed; scope/escalation and QA proposals remain
  proposals until their own human review. No automated audits or rollout.

# Local review operation

These scripts use a durable demo directory containing index.html, lab.json and evidence/. Use the configured output directory from TEAM-INSTALL.md. Never replace a current review with a triage-only refresh when the user requested actual reviews.

## Start the existing UI

Run `python <skill>/scripts/serve_review_lab.py --directory <demo>` and open the printed HTTP URL in Codex. It reuses a matching server or starts a hidden static Python server at 127.0.0.1:8769. A conflicting server is left alone. Keep the origin stable: file:/// and other ports have different browser storage. This does not launch Codex tasks, refresh PRs, or install an auto-start service.

## Extra diff context

After pinning and inspecting Git revisions, run `python <skill>/scripts/collect_diff_context.py --input <lab.json> --output <lab.json> --repo <inspection-checkout>`, then use the normal renderer. This reads Git objects without checkout changes. Each hunk gets at most ten matching unchanged lines on each side, bounded by adjacent hunks. Missing/binary/non-UTF8 objects omit expansion. The renderer keeps this context out of changed-line totals and default layer context exports. Recollect after revisions change; do not reuse old arrays on new heads.

## Separate PR checklist audit

The unified skill includes `scripts/collect_audit_queue.py`, `scripts/build_pr_checklist.py` and `assets/pr-checklist-template.html`. Both scripts take `--directory <demo>`. The collector accepts `--repository DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph` and `--reviewer authenticated`; search and prior queue membership are limited to that repository. Collection is GitHub read-only and needs authenticated gh. It checks direct pending requests and re-request timelines, including PRs from the existing queue. Respect API pagination/truncation limits; do not claim completeness if collection is incomplete.

The builder consumes lab.json, evidence/audit-queue.json, evidence/current/queue.json and evidence/body-audit.json. Retrieve each PR body and assess Loom URLs, other video URLs, scope-check statements and local-review statements before rendering. Preserve exact supporting text and collection timestamps; checked claims are not independent verification. Body evidence uses prs entries keyed by url with updatedAt/fetched_at, loom {status, urls, other_video_urls}, scope_check and local_review {status, evidence:[], notes:[]}; statement statuses are claimed, unchecked, partial, missing. Preserve the fetched_at timestamp on the body-audit envelope. Never invent missing evidence to satisfy the schema.

The audit excludes tests and __tests__ directory segments from additions + deletions, preserves gross/test totals, and flags >500 and >700 strictly. It reuses matching local PR completions. It is a separate artifact, not a review-depth replacement.

Normal render also writes archives.html and notes.html beside the review index.
The main review header hides Archives and Examples, Notes and To-dos, Export notes & progress, and Import state under Menu. The auxiliary pages retain their own page navigation.
Archives lists safe local related_views except the current queue. Notes and To-dos
stores freeform text and checkable/removable tasks under mg-review-lab:desk-notes:v1
in localStorage, independently of PR progress; regeneration never erases that storage.
Provide JSON export and visible storage errors. User text is rendered as text, not HTML.
These pages remain local and do not send provider messages or change PRs.

Retain the Review lab brand header on Archives and Examples and Notes and To-dos. Omit MVP0 and Your local review desk everywhere. Keep page navigation below the header. The brand returns to the review queue; the theme toggle shares mg-review-theme with the main page.

Menu export/import includes deskNotes {notes,tasks:[{id,text,done}]} from the Notes and To-dos page. Import replaces desk notes when supplied, preserves them for legacy exports without deskNotes, and accepts standalone review-desk-notes.json exports. Validate notes/tasks before applying imported state. Open notes pages refresh via storage events.

# Policy lab-1

Project/milestone context informs value: retrieve intended outcome, target date, status and acceptance dependencies. Verified release-critical contributions can justify priority with a source/date. Membership alone is not a blocker. Milestone progress is reported Linear progress, not the fraction of PRs reviewed here. Never boost priority merely because a historical target date has passed.

Priority and next action are independent. Preserve readiness gates and the analyst's next action. Findings describe defects, not urgency.

- Explicit incident/release urgency with source evidence may receive P0/P1.
- An evidenced downstream blocker receives P1 in the suggested review order, with exact count and source. This is a review-order suggestion, not a claim of business urgency.
- Others default to P2 with sufficient intent, otherwise Unknown. P3 requires explicit low-value assessment, never missing data.
- Within bands, use confirmed acyclic prerequisites before dependents, then downstream count and lower effort. Preserve cycles and conflicts visibly; inferred overlap cannot establish merge order.

S/M/L effort is a labeled structural estimate from files/changed lines. Do not invent minutes. Risk comes from the reviewer rationale, not LOC. Missing ownership evidence means no reviewer suggestion. Close candidates need explicit duplicate/superseded evidence or documented human assessment; age alone is insufficient. Exclude incident, security, pinned and release-critical work from automatic nominations.

Manual priority overrides are local, retain calculated reasons, and can be cleared. Export/import retains them for the same dataset identity. No provider writes.

Run it locally and record it in the PR. That's the version that actually speeds up Michael's review. Sharing your review-lab output wouldn't save him any work.

**Why the output isn't worth sharing:**
- Review-lab is a reviewer's local tool. It builds a single offline HTML page plus a `lab.json` on your machine, and keeps notes in your browser. It never posts to GitHub or Linear.
- Michael's copy can't import your results. When he refreshes his queue, it re-reviews every PR at its current commit. Your assessment would also be a self-review, so he'd redo it anyway.
- Don't attach it to the PR. `discourse-graph` is public, review-lab is private, and its output includes Linear ticket comments and project context.

**What his tool reads from your PR:** its checklist flags any PR body with no Loom, no scope check or no local-review statement. It also flags PRs over 500 changed lines, not counting files in `tests/` folders. The "Local delegated full review" section in your template is where a review-lab line goes. name: mg-pr-review-html
description: Review a GitHub pull request against its diff and Linear intent, then generate a visual HTML review connecting scope and specs to implementation, evidence, findings, and an ordered walkthrough. Use for PR reviews, HTML reviews, review one-pagers, or review-plus-explanation requests.
---

# PR Review HTML

Create a read-only, evidence-based PR review. Never change GitHub state, the PR branch, or the active worktree. Never launch a nested `codex` process.

## Workflow

1. Use `dg-engineering-writing-style` from the owning Discourse Graph repository for all review prose. For the portable team pilot, resolve and verify its explicit `writing_skill` configuration through [team setup](../mg-review-lab/references/team-setup.md). If the skill is unavailable, report the missing dependency; do not substitute a personal writing style.
2. Confirm the PR belongs to the current DiscourseGraphs repository. Non-DG targets are rejected.
3. Prepare a detached worktree from the repository root. Checkouts live under `<repository>/local/reviews/.worktrees/<run>/worktree`; manifests, JSON, and retrieved context live under `local/reviews/.runs/<run>/`. Both are locally ignored:

```powershell
python "<package>/skills/mg-pr-review-html/scripts/generate_pr_review.py" prepare --pr 123
```

Add `--linear-ticket ENG-1855` when the request names a ticket. Omit `--pr` only when the current branch has a PR. Preparation otherwise searches the PR description, then the first three PR comments for a Linear reference. Inspect other relevant links in PR metadata and retrieved context.

4. Read the printed manifest, generated instructions, and schema completely.
5. If a Linear candidate was discovered, retrieve the full issue and every comment with the connected Linear read tools. Follow comment pagination. Read directly relevant linked tickets, scope/spec docs, and design decisions. Save retrieved material in `run_dir/context/`; put source metadata and requirement assessments in the review JSON. Record inaccessible or conflicting sources. Never update Linear or external documents.
6. Review only the manifest's pinned base-to-head diff in its detached worktree. Inspect surrounding code and run proportionate checks.
7. Write one JSON object at `review_json` that exactly matches the schema.
8. Finalize the review:

```powershell
python "<package>/skills/mg-pr-review-html/scripts/generate_pr_review.py" finalize --manifest <manifest-path>
```

Finalization always removes the temporary worktree unless preparation used
`--keep-worktree`. If the review JSON is invalid, it preserves the small run artifacts
for correction but still removes the worktree. A later `prepare` also reaps abandoned,
non-retained worktrees from runs older than 12 hours.

9. Report every generated HTML path. Open a page only when asked.

## Worktree maintenance

Run these from the repository root using the same `generate_pr_review.py` script:

```powershell
python "<package>/skills/mg-pr-review-html/scripts/generate_pr_review.py" list
python "<package>/skills/mg-pr-review-html/scripts/generate_pr_review.py" cleanup --stale --dry-run
python "<package>/skills/mg-pr-review-html/scripts/generate_pr_review.py" cleanup --stale
```

Use `cleanup --all` for all non-retained runs, or `--pr 123` to narrow a batch. `--dry-run` prints paths without removal. Batch cleanup skips `--keep-worktree` runs; clean a retained run explicitly with `--manifest <path>`. Run artifacts are preserved by default. Add `--remove-artifacts` to remove that run's JSON/context too; rendered HTML remains.

Older version 2 manifests still support cleanup of their exact system-temp checkouts. Cleanup does not scan/delete arbitrary temp folders. Failed Git removal and unregistered directories containing files are preserved for inspection, with an actionable path. Use the Git-aware cleanup command rather than deleting a registered worktree in Explorer.

## Review contract

- Apply `references/codex-review-rubric.md` as the authoritative finding rubric. Only its output shape is replaced by `assets/review-output-schema.json` (version 2).
- Report actionable problems introduced by the PR. Keep findings diff-anchored, with evidence and a practical correction. Requirements reference finding IDs instead of repeating the bug.
- Organize the page around behavioral change, intent and evidence, reviewer attention, and one ordered walkthrough. Omit empty sections. Do not generate separate changed-area summaries, review maps, or beginner lessons.
- Prefer visual explanations when they reduce reading: multiple complementary visuals are welcome. Choose graph/architecture, state, sequence, decision table, before/after pseudocode, or actual UI screenshots. Follow [visual guidance](references/visual-explanations.md). Do not force a diagram for a trivial change or repeat the same explanation in several formats.
- Derive requirements from retrieved tickets/specs, not the implementation. Distinguish implementation assessment from verification. Cite sources and pinned code; link exact checks by ID. Show source conflicts and unexpected scope as explicit reviewer decisions.
- Keep review findings and verification status separate. Failed checks, unrun checks, unverified requirements, and missing intent context remain visible near the header even when no blocking bug was found.
- Use one sentence for the change summary. Short prose and concrete examples are preferred; no bullet quotas. Keep walkthrough items focused on one behavior with a reason to inspect it.
- Background and quizzes are opt-in for an explicit learning request. `learning` and `quiz` are optional and collapsed; no fixed question count.
- Wrap identifiers, paths, fields, and commands in backticks. Use light inline formatting where useful.
- Keep raw ticket descriptions/comments in local context artifacts, outside the HTML. Link PR, source documents, branches, and pinned commits. Preserve run artifacts on success while removing the temporary worktree.
- Keep generated artifacts local. Do not post comments, submit reviews, apply fixes, alter branches, add labels, or modify tracked ignore files.

## Failure handling

- Stop if `git` or `gh` is unavailable or unauthenticated.
- Linear failures do not block the code review. Record the exact failure in `linear_context`.
- If finalization rejects the JSON, fix only the invalid structured output and retry.
- If any step after preparation cannot complete, clean the worktree before returning while
  preserving diagnostic artifacts:

```powershell
python "<package>/skills/mg-pr-review-html/scripts/generate_pr_review.py" cleanup --manifest <manifest-path> --keep-artifacts
```

## Resources

- `references/review-prompt.md`: PR-specific review and writing requirements.
- `references/codex-review-rubric.md`: finding threshold and review behavior.
- `assets/review-output-schema.json`: structured review contract.
- `scripts/generate_pr_review.py`: prepare, finalize, and cleanup workflow.
- `scripts/render_review.py`: self-contained HTML renderer.


## Primer presentation

Use GitHub Primer styling for review HTML, with bundled semantic light/dark tokens and native HTML controls. Follow [Primer design guidance](../mg-review-lab/references/primer-design.md). Preserve offline exports and existing review interactions.

When producing the shared review lab, include an authored Pseudocode tab for every queued PR. Follow [the lab pseudocode contract](../mg-review-lab/references/pseudocode.md), inspecting the pinned code and retaining failure paths and review caveats. Generate through the canonical lab renderer rather than patching HTML.
---
# Shared record v1

Optional `project_context` records project ID/name/URL/status/summary, milestone ID/name/summary, target date, reported progress, assignment source, PR contribution and independent observation date/status. Unknown or unassigned milestones are explicit. `attach-context` accepts `{observed_at, issues:[{id,projectId,project,projectMilestone,url}], context:{projectId:{title,url,status,description,milestones:[{id,name,description,targetDate,progress}]}}}`. Preserve historical context dates even when the PR review is newer. No rank is changed by this adapter.

The `validate` command enforces identities, SHAs, hunk/layer references and visual targets. Evidence is not approval.

Top level: `version:1`, `title`, `generated_at`, `snapshot_note`, `prs`, `dependencies`, `provenance`.

Each PR: `key` (owner/repo#number), `repository`, `number`, `url`, `title`, `base_sha`, `head_sha`, `observed_at`, `freshness` (historical/current/stale/unknown), nullable `current_head_sha`, `intent`, `ticket`, `mode`, `risk`, `readiness`, `next_action`, `priority`, `effort`, `reviewers`, `close_candidate`, `requirements`, `findings`, `checks`, `decisions`, `layers`, `files`.

Priority: `level`, `reason`, `basis`, `confidence`. Effort: `band`, `reason`. Reviewer/close recommendations require reason and source URL. Current freshness requires matching reviewed/current heads and a recent provider observation. Rendering does not refresh evidence.

Files: `id`, `path`, `old_path`, `status`, `hunks`, `notice`. Hunks: `id`, old/new starts/counts, `lines` containing `kind` (context/add/delete/meta), nullable old/new line numbers and exact `text`. Capture all hunks and binary notices. All files is the authoritative coverage view; layers may share hunks.

Layers: `id`, `title`, `summary`, `basis` (authored/structural), `hunk_ids`, `requirement_ids`, `finding_ids`, `check_ids`, `visuals`. Requirements: `id`, `text`, `source_url`, `assessment`, `verification`, `layer_ids`, `check_ids`. Filename matches cannot establish verification. Preserve source conflicts and non-goals.

Visuals have `kind`, `title`, `caption`. Flow/architecture/sequence/state use `nodes:[{id,label,detail,layer_id}]` and `edges:[{from,to,label}]`. Pseudocode uses `before`,`after`, optional `layer_id`. Decision tables use `columns`,`rows`. UI comparisons use embedded image data URIs `before_src`,`after_src` and meaningful `before_alt`,`after_alt`. Author from inspected behavior, not filenames.

Dependencies: `before`,`after` PR keys, `kind`,`confidence`,`summary`,`url`. External keys render as external prerequisites. Only explicit high-confidence blockers/stacks affect automatic order. Importers label heuristic mappings and preserve old evidence.

Browser progress is snapshot-specific. `compare` produces candidates for evidence-based rereview, not automatic fixed findings. Private source text stays outside the HTML.

## Narrative record

Optional `narrative` is bound to base/head and contains authored explanatory text and verified diff targets. See [the narrative guide](narrative.md) for fields, attribution and validation. It does not change review depth, findings, checks or readiness.

`narrative.format_version: 2` adds optional structured `example`, before/after
`pseudocode`, and disclosed `verification` text. Examples and pseudocode target a
validated narrative step through `step_id`. Version 2 without these blocks shows
before/after prose. Missing format version means the legacy flow layout. This does
not change the top-level record version or browser progress identity.

## Review execution

Optional `review_execution` records `base_sha`, `head_sha`, `reviewed_at`, `depth`, and `summary`. Individual checks retain command, status, observed execution and evidence URL. Optional `intent_source_text` preserves full acceptance wording when requirements are grouped. Such requirements set `source_kind: paraphrased`; omit it for formatting-normalized ticket text. A narrative or imported provider check does not set review execution.

---
name: mg-pr-review-queue-html
description: Triage a queue of related GitHub pull requests, review selected PRs against Linear intent at a risk-proportionate depth, and produce a polished offline HTML dashboard with compact evidence-backed review capsules. Use for PR review queues, ordered multi-PR review, rereviews, or individual PR reviews where reducing context switching matters.
---

# PR Review Queue HTML

Review GitHub pull requests without changing GitHub, Linear, the source checkout, or its active worktree. Produce local, self-contained HTML as the primary deliverable. Never post comments, submit reviews, change labels or branches, update Linear, apply fixes, or launch a nested model process.

## Choose the mode

- `triage`: mandatory first pass for a queue. Gather only enough evidence to assess intent, ticket linkage, change surface, risk, readiness, dependencies, semantic center, and next action.
- `standard`: normal selected-PR review. Validate the behavioral contract, intended scope, semantic center, tests, and actionable introduced findings.
- `deep`: standard review plus wider call-site tracing, richer explanation, diagrams, selected excerpts, and additional proportionate checks. Use only for high-risk or explicitly requested depth.
- `rereview`: compare the last reviewed immutable head SHA with the current head and revisit unresolved findings. Do not rebuild unchanged explanation.

Read [references/modes.md](references/modes.md) for the selected mode. Read [references/data-contract.md](references/data-contract.md) before writing or validating structured review data. For a performance/cache evaluation, also read [references/evaluation.md](references/evaluation.md). Apply [references/codex-review-rubric.md](references/codex-review-rubric.md) whenever deciding whether an issue qualifies as a finding.

## Two-pass workflow

1. Resolve the local repository without modifying it. Use a temporary clone/worktree for code inspection. Pin every PR to its GitHub-reported head SHA and compute the merge base against the fetched base in that isolated clone.
2. In pass 1, triage every requested PR. Record draft/CI state, unresolved decisions, missing intent, ticket-link status, diff size and areas, likely semantic center, risks, dependencies, and a recommended next action. Do not perform deep explanation or exhaustive checks.
3. Perform the mandatory scope check for each PR:
   - Prefer a Linear ticket explicitly supplied by the user for that PR.
   - Always discover references from GitHub metadata, even with an explicit selection. Retain contradictory candidates and their sources as ambiguity evidence while keeping the explicit ticket selected; make missing or multiple candidates prominent.
   - Retrieve the issue, comments, blockers/blocked-by links, parent/sub-issues, and relevant project or milestone context with read-only Linear tools. Preserve provenance. Failure to retrieve Linear never aborts code review.
   - Derive intended outcomes, acceptance criteria, and explicit non-goals. Compare them with the immutable base-to-head diff, separating implemented scope, missing scope, and out-of-scope additions.
   - Promote an actionable scope gap to a normal diff-anchored finding only when it satisfies the review rubric. Keep ambiguity and non-actionable gaps out of findings.
4. Order the queue only when evidence supports it. Explicit Linear relations outrank stacked-base and explicit GitHub references; those outrank structural or semantic inference. Label inferred relations low-confidence, preserve provenance, expose conflicts/cycles, and never manufacture a total order.
5. Select pass-2 mode and PRs from triage. Match effort to risk and readiness. If draft state, failing CI, missing intent, or an unresolved upstream decision makes detailed review premature, say so and recommend the next action.
6. Find the small semantic center of each selected diff and recommend the few files or areas requiring human attention. Run proportionate checks in the isolated worktree and record exact commands and outcomes.
7. Write one review-package JSON object following `assets/review-package.schema.json`, validate it, then render the queue dashboard. The first screen of each PR capsule must cover intent, behavioral contract, implementation path, scope alignment, primary risks, reading order, checks, readiness, and verdict. Put neutral comprehension before critical assessment.
8. Keep generated artifacts under a user-selected local output directory or a temporary directory. Do not edit tracked ignore files. Report all generated paths.

Don't merge them yet. Nothing would be lost, but you're right that the diffs would get messy, and it's worse than you thought: #1577's base isn't `main`, it's #1576. The full stack is:

```
main ← #1576 ENG-2061 (waiting on Michael) ← #1577 1/3 ✓ ← #1578 2/3 ✓ ← #1579 3/3 (waiting on Michael)
```

**If you merge #1577 now:** GitHub squashes it into the ENG-2061 branch, not `main`. #1576's diff then grows to include ENG-1824 part 1 while Michael is reviewing it as an ENG-2061 refactor. Merging #1578 would land in part 1's branch in the same way. The `main` rules (squash only, one approval) only protect `main`, so GitHub won't stop either merge.

Both approvals are from Michael, so the whole stack is really waiting on #1576 and #1579.

**When #1576 is approved, merge from the bottom up:**
1. Squash-merge #1576 into `main`.
2. Change #1577's base to `main`. GitHub won't do this for you, because branch deletion on merge is off here.
3. Merge `main` into the #1577 branch with a plain merge, no force-push. Squash merging creates a new commit, so #1577 still carries #1576's original commits. Until you merge `main` in, its diff would show ENG-2061's changes again.
4. Squash-merge #1577, then repeat steps 2–4 for #1578, then #1579.

Michael's approvals survive those pushes, because stale-review dismissal is off. The `main` ruleset also has `require_extra_approval_for_unattributed_changes` turned on. I'm not sure whether it treats a merge-from-`main` commit as unattributed, so it might ask for a re-approval.

The ordering also matters for Michael's tool: review-lab treats a changed base as "full review required". If he reviews #1579 now and its base moves later, his lab will flag it for a full re-review. The less churn option is to get #1576 approved, merge #1576 → #1577 → #1578, and only then have him review #1579.

On PR #1216 (ENG-2019), relocating Obsidian's `metadata as Record<string, any>` casts made CI's eslint check annotate the "pre-existing" `no-explicit-any` warnings on the new lines. sid flagged them ("these types of eslint errors").

**Why:** The GitHub eslint annotator attributes warnings to whoever last touched the line. "Warning-neutral relocation" is not neutral on the PR — the reviewer sees new warnings.

**How to apply:** When a swap/extraction moves lines that carry lint warnings, fix the underlying issue in the same PR instead of preserving the pattern. For `Json` metadata access: narrow with `x !== null && typeof x === "object" && !Array.isArray(x)` — TS then resolves property access natively, no casts. Check `npx eslint` on touched files against the OLD count and expect it to go down, not stay equal.

**The exact CI mechanism** (`.github/workflows/ci.yaml`, `lint-changed-files`, verified 2026-07-27): eslint runs on whole changed *files*, but the result goes through `reviewdog -filter-mode=added -fail-level=warning`. So warnings on lines the diff does NOT touch never fail the job — only added/changed lines do. Practical consequence: adding a one-token edit to a file full of pre-existing warnings is safe, and `npx eslint --max-warnings 0 <file>` failing locally is not by itself a CI failure. Confirm which lines the warnings sit on (`diff` your change against `origin/main`) before spending effort on unrelated ones.

---
name: think-like-michael
description: Evaluate code decisions through Michael's tech lead mental model
user_invocable: true
---

<skill-prompt>
You are reviewing code through Michael's (mdroidian) tech lead lens. This is NOT a lint pass — it's a design-thinking pass. Read the current git diff (staged + unstaged), then evaluate against these 10 questions that represent how Michael approaches every code change.

Note: Much of the code is now written by AI agents (Claude Code, Devin). Michael doesn't care who wrote it — he reviews the diff the same way. But agent-written code has specific failure modes that show up in his reviews.

For each concern found, explain the *thinking* behind it, not just the rule. Michael's voice is direct, specific, and always explains the "why."

---

## The 10 Questions

### 1. Can every change be explained?
For every hunk in the diff, the author should be able to say in one sentence why it changed. Michael's most common recent feedback is asking "why?" about changes that exist in the diff with no clear purpose — removals, reorderings, pattern breaks, eslint-disables that the author can't justify because an agent made them incidentally. If a change isn't part of the task and can't be explained, it should be reverted or annotated in the PR.

> *"Why is this being removed? Is it being replaced with something?"* — PR #784
> *"What was the purpose of this change?"* — PR #696
> *"What is the purpose of re-ordering these?"* — PR #696
> *"Why do we need to resort to this disable? What did you try to properly fix it?"* — PR #765

### 2. Does this already exist in the repo?
Before any new function, type, component, or npm package — search the codebase. Michael holds a mental map of the repo and expects the team to build one too. The worst outcome is two slightly different versions of the same thing. Extend existing code before creating new code.

### 3. Does this need to exist?
Every line is a liability. If a useEffect, wrapper div, state variable, cache layer, or export can be removed without breaking anything — it shouldn't be there. Don't cache cheap queries. Don't memoize simple filters. Don't wrap in `<div>` when `<>` or nothing will do. Don't export what isn't used elsewhere. Don't assign a const to the same value that already exists above.

> *"Why do we need to assign another const to the same value as above?"* — PR #696

### 4. Is this the right size?
Agent-written code tends to be verbose. Michael pushes for conciseness. If a component or function is large, it probably should be half the size. If a validate function returns a string or undefined but is named like it returns boolean, the naming and design need rethinking.

> *"Let's cut this in half."* — PR #696
> *"I wonder if `validate` could be renamed to better reflect its return value."* — PR #696

### 5. Does this run at the right time and frequency?
Trace the execution path. Code in observers, init functions, and top-level effects runs on every page/load/navigation. Migration code should run once (on enable). Don't duplicate queries that already ran upstream. If something expensive is already memoized upstream, a downstream filter doesn't also need memoizing.

### 6. Does it fetch once and manage locally?
The pattern: query from source once → store in React state → on user action, update local state AND write to source → never re-fetch to get data you already have. Re-fetching causes race conditions and unnecessary latency. Use return values from create/update operations.

### 7. Do the types and names tell the truth?
`any` is a lie. An unnecessary `?.` is a lie — it tells the next dev "this can be null" when it can't, causing defensive code for impossible cases. Type assertions (`as`) override the compiler — use type guards instead. Names must match semantics: `defaultValue` ≠ `initialValue` ≠ `value` in React. If a name would cause the reader to guess wrong, it's broken.

### 8. Does it follow existing patterns?
New code should match how similar things are already done in the repo. Use Blueprint components, Tailwind (not inline styles), arrow functions, roamjs-components where they exist. Don't introduce a new way to do something the codebase already does. If a panel follows a pattern, don't break it without a reason.

> *"Why is this panel breaking the pattern with `setter`? What is the reason/need for this?"* — PR #804
> *"roamjs?"* — PR #784 (meaning: use roamjs-components, not custom code)

### 9. What does the user see?
Silent failures erode trust. Console errors mean nothing to users — use Toasts. When data is sent to external servers, inform the user explicitly. "False negative" states (showing "no results" when we didn't actually search) are worse than errors. If a feature isn't ready for users, gate it behind a flag.

### 10. Does this belong in this PR? Is the future noted?
One problem per PR. If you find a bigger issue, create a ticket and move on. Accept pragmatic solutions but document the debt: a TODO with context ("when we migrate to X, this needs Y") beats a perfect abstraction that blocks shipping. Some decisions need a meeting, not a commit.

---

## Agent Review Anti-Patterns — DO NOT USE THESE

When you find something during analysis, do not soften it with weasel phrases. These are cop-outs that bury real findings:

- **"Not harmful, just unnecessary"** → If it's unnecessary, it fails Question #3. Say: "This is dead code. Remove it." Then explain why it's dead.
- **"Acceptable for consistency"** → Consistency is not a reason to keep code that does nothing. If a generic wrapper is a no-op for a specific call site, that's not consistency, it's cargo-culting.
- **"Minor note" / "not worth changing"** → If you wrote it down, decide: is it actionable (flag it) or genuinely out of scope (say why and move on)? No middle ground.
- **Noting facts without drawing the conclusion** → If you trace that a function always returns `boolean`, and `false ?? fallback` evaluates to `false`, then SAY "this fallback is dead code." Don't list the facts and then look away. Follow the chain to its end.

The rule: if you have all the information that leads to a finding, you MUST state the finding explicitly. "I noticed X but it's fine" is not a review — it's a missed catch.

## Output Format

For each concern:
- **File:line** — location
- **Question #** — which of the 10
- **Michael would say:** — in his voice (direct, starts with "Let's..." or a question, always explains why)
- **What to do** — concrete action

If the diff is clean against all 10 questions, say so explicitly. Don't manufacture concerns.
</skill-prompt>

name: review-like-michael
description: Review the current diff against mdroidian's review patterns
user_invocable: true
---

<skill-prompt>
Review the current git diff (staged + unstaged) against the following checklist. This checklist was distilled from 530+ real PR review comments by mdroidian (including open PRs as of Feb 2026). Only flag issues that actually appear in the diff — don't invent problems.

Note: Most code is now written by AI agents. Michael reviews the diff the same way regardless — but agent code has specific failure modes (incidental changes, pattern breaks, verbose output) reflected in rules 1, 10, 11, and 14.

For each issue found, output:
- **File:line** — the location
- **Rule** — which rule it violates (by number)
- **What the reviewer would say** — written in Matt's voice (direct, specific, usually starts with "Let's..." or asks "Why?")
- **Fix** — the concrete change

If the diff is clean, say so.

---

## The Rules

1. **Can every change be explained?** For each hunk, can you say in one sentence why it changed? Unexplained removals, reorderings, pattern breaks, and eslint-disables get flagged. If a change isn't part of the task, revert it or annotate it. "Why is this being removed?" "What was the purpose of this change?" "Why do we need to resort to this disable?"

2. **Does this already exist?** Search the repo before creating new functions, types, components, or installing new packages. Reuse existing helpers (`getDiscourseNodes`, `extractRef`, `getNewDiscourseNodeText`, etc.), roamjs-components, and already-installed npm packages.

3. **Is this actually needed?** If you can't explain what breaks without a piece of code (a useEffect, wrapper div, state variable, cache layer, redundant const), remove it. Don't cache cheap queries. Don't memoize simple filters. Don't assign a const to the same value that already exists.

4. **What runs on every page load?** Migration/setup code runs once (on enable), not every load. Don't duplicate queries that already ran upstream. If it's in an observer or init function, it's on the hot path.

5. **Fetch once, manage locally.** Query settings/config once, manage in React state. Use return values from create/update operations instead of re-fetching. Re-fetching causes race conditions.

6. **No `any`, no lying optional chains.** Types must reflect reality. Prefer type guards over assertions. Don't add `?.` or `|| ""` if the value can't be null — it misleads about error paths. Use existing types and Zod schemas.

7. **Names must say what they mean.** `defaultValue` ≠ `initialValue` ≠ `value` — use the right one. Function names should reflect return types (a "validate" that returns a string should be "getValidationError"). Error messages and labels must be specific. If renaming without behavior change, explain in the PR.

8. **Only export what's intended for reuse.** Unexported = internal. If only used in one file, don't export it.

9. **Colocate with usage.** Code used by one component lives in that component. Move to shared utils only when actually reused. Follow established placement patterns.

10. **Follow existing patterns.** Blueprint components, roamjs-components, Tailwind (not inline styles), arrow functions, sentence case for labels, Prettier formatting. Don't break an established pattern without explaining why. "Why is this panel breaking the pattern with `setter`?"

11. **Keep it concise and reviewable.** Agent code tends to be verbose — cut it in half. No unnecessary wrappers that inflate diffs. Don't reorganize surrounding code in a feature PR. `<>` over unnecessary `<div>`. eslint-disable on the specific line, not the whole file.

12. **Gate unfinished features.** Behind a flag. Conditional on parent feature being enabled. "If we merge this, is it ready for Pilot Users?"

13. **Think about what the user sees.** Toast for user-facing errors (not just console). Inform users when data is sent externally. Test with CSS plugins disabled.

14. **If the reviewer can't follow it, simplify.** Confusing prop interplay → flatten. Nested ternaries → explicit conditionals. If a function is big, it should probably be half the size.

15. **Prove it works.** Loom video for user-facing changes (zoom in ~50% for large monitors). Test by removing things you're unsure about.

16. **Stop and discuss when needed.** Design decisions → meeting. Unsure → flag, don't guess. Out-of-scope → Linear ticket, not scope creep.
</skill-prompt>

6	
7	<skill-prompt>
8	Run a pre-PR review of the current change set. This is NOT a checklist to ponder — it is a sequence of verification steps with pass/fail outcomes. You must actually run the greps/traces; "I believe this is fine" without having looked is a failed step. Built from an autopsy of 97 real reviewer comments (2026-03→07) — 46 violated rules a previous skill already "had" but never enforced; recall is not verification — and refreshed 2026-08-28 against the 2026-07→08 corpus (~200 human review comments across sid's and teammates' PRs).
9	
10	Required reading before step 1 (both live in `<repo-root>/.claude/context/`, repo root `/mnt/data/projects/discourse-graph` — reachable by absolute path from any worktree):
11	- `engineering-context.md` — team philosophies and hard-learned lessons (the *why* behind every check below)
12	- `db-domain-invariants.md` — current schema/data-layer facts (the data-layer pass checks the diff against every entry)
13	
14	## Mode gate (run FIRST, before Step 0)
15	
16	Decide which mode this run needs. This is a judgment call you make from evidence — not a rule to apply mechanically, and not something to take on faith from the dispatching prompt (dispatch prompts are written fresh each run and can get this wrong in either direction):
17	- Evidence a full pass already ran on this PR: a previous run's line-anchored annotations posted on the PR, existing review threads answering a prior findings report, or the dispatcher naming a last-reviewed SHA.
18	- Default when a full pass ran and the commits since only answer review feedback: Re-review mode below.
19	- A full pass on a follow-up push can still be the right call when there's genuine reason — the delta added surface beyond the feedback (the escape hatch below), the base moved under the branch, prior coverage looks doubtful or stale, or enough rounds have accumulated that the whole PR deserves fresh eyes. If you judge that, run full and say why.
20	- The first line of your output states the chosen mode and the reasoning — that's what keeps the choice reviewable, whichever way it goes.
21	
22	## Step 0 — Inventory
23	
24	The change set is the FULL PR diff: `git diff <base>...HEAD` (merge-base three-dot against the PR's base branch — the stack parent for stacked PRs, else main) plus staged/unstaged changes. Never review only the latest commits: reviewers see the whole PR, and code that landed on the branch before this run is still your surface. (Exception: Re-review mode below.) Classify changed files:
25	- **DATA**: `packages/database/**`, `*.sql`, any file containing a Supabase/PostgREST call (`.from(`), datalog query, or cross-app contract type
26	- **FRONTEND**: `apps/roam/**`, `apps/obsidian/**`, `apps/website/**` UI code
27	- **OTHER**: tests, docs, config
28	
29	Steps 2 and 3 are scoped: skip the data-layer pass if no DATA files changed; skip the frontend pass if no FRONTEND files changed. Never skip steps 1 and 4.
30	
31	## Re-review mode (follow-up pushes)
32	
33	If a full pre-pr-review already ran on this PR and this run covers a follow-up push (fixes after a review round or a previous run's findings), do NOT repeat the full sequence:
34	
35	- Change set = `git diff <last-reviewed-sha>...HEAD` — the commits since the state the previous round covered, not the whole PR again.
36	- **Findings closure first.** For every finding from the previous run and every reviewer/bot comment since: re-run the SPECIFIC check that produced it and report fixed / not-fixed / deferred+ticket per item. A fix claimed without re-verification is a failed step; a UI fix additionally gets re-driven (existing rule).
37	- Run steps 1–3 mechanically on the delta only, with Step 0's DATA/FRONTEND scoping applied to the delta. Step 4 shrinks to: every new hunk maps to the review feedback or the ticket, and the bot-comment gate on comments the new push attracted.
38	- Skip re-reading the context docs unless the delta touches DATA/FRONTEND files and they aren't already in context.
39	- Escape hatch: if the "follow-up" adds new surface (rebase onto a moved base, new feature code, a refactor beyond what was asked), it is not a re-review — run the full sequence on the full PR diff.
40	
41	## Step 1 — Mechanical sweeps (always run; each is an action, not a question)
42	
43	1a. **Reuse gate.** List every NEW named thing in the diff (function, type, component, constant, enum, marker string). For each, run a grep across `apps/roam/src/utils`, `packages/utils`, `packages/database/src`, and sibling files for the core operation or shape. Report what you searched and what you found. A new thing duplicating an existing one is a finding. Special case: every inline string-literal union (`"X" | "Y"`) gets its members grepped in `packages/database/src/dbTypes.ts`; members matching a generated enum → must use `Enums<"…">`.
44	
45	1b. **Justification sweep.** For every added default value, optional prop/field, state variable, fallback (`?? x`, `|| x`), and kept-through-refactor line: name the concrete code path that exercises it. Trace return types through call sites — if a function always returns `T`, a `?? fallback` at its call site is dead code; say so. No path → finding: delete it.
46	
47	1c. **Literal hoist.** Repeated or typo-prone string literals (prop keys, selectors, attribute names, ids) appearing more than once or shared with other files → must be a named constant defined once.
48	
49	1d. **Type honesty.** For every `as`, `any`, `unknown`, `!` (non-null assertion), `?.`, `void`, and `|| default` in the diff: can the value actually be null/absent there? Verify against the type at its source, don't guess. Assertion where a guard or upstream fix is possible → finding. A `!` that must survive gets an inline comment saying why it's safe — mdroidian flags every bare `!` (#1329, #1324).
50	
51	1e. **Explainability.** For each hunk: one sentence, why is this here in service of the ticket? Reorderings, reformats, removals, and leftover scaffolding you can't explain → finding: revert.
52	
53	1f. **Call-graph pass (review the resulting system, not the diff).** For every exported symbol added or modified, and every function parameter added: grep ALL call sites across `apps/` and `packages/` and read them. Findings:
54	- a parameter that only one caller supplies (or that every caller could omit) → internalize or remove it
55	- a wrapper that after this change only renames/forwards or adds one trivial field → collapse it into its caller
56	- an export with zero external consumers → unexport
57	- an existing caller whose behavior silently changes (check what it did with the old return shape — e.g. did it append `Z` to a timestamp you now normalize?)
58	Reviewers read the post-state code, not the diff; a hunk that looks justified in isolation can leave the system with dead indirection.
59	
60	1g. **Comment audit.** List every comment line ADDED by the diff. Delete any that restates the code or narrates the change — "Claude, chill on the comments" is a real review quote, left twice (#1222, #1321), and "some unnecessary comments here" a third time (#1292). A comment referencing context not present in the file (another PR, a discussion, another platform's behavior) either becomes self-contained or dies: reviewers reply "What is F12?" / "What is the same reason?" to comments they can't parse cold (#1315, #1292, #1284). Keep only comments stating a constraint the code can't show.
61	
62	1h. **Second-lookup check.** For every new fetch, map-build, `.find`, or helper lookup: trace where its input data was constructed — was the looked-up value already present there (on the row, the batch, an upstream type)? If yes → thread the field through the pipeline types instead of re-deriving downstream. (#1266: importer re-fetched `schema_id` that `SharedNode` already carried; #1317: `getFormatByNodeTypeUid()` second lookup when `matchingNodeType.format` was in hand at the construction site.)
63	
64	1i. **Workflow injection (only if `.github/workflows/` changed).** Any `${{ inputs.* }}` / `${{ github.event.* }}` interpolated directly into a `run:` script is shell injection — pass it through `env:` and use a quoted variable, validated against a fully anchored pattern (#1253).
65	
66	## Step 2 — Data-layer pass (only if DATA files changed)
67	
68	2a. Open `db-domain-invariants.md` and check the diff against EVERY entry. For each entry state: applies / doesn't apply / VIOLATION. Do not summarize the file — walk it.
69	
70	2b. **Provenance trace.** For every value read from a PostgREST response or datalog result used in the diff: name the source column, grep its type in `packages/database/supabase/schemas/*.sql`, then judge the code handling it (timestamps are the known killer — naive UTC, no `Z`).
71	
72	2c. **Query review.** For every `.from(...)` chain (new or modified): required domain filters present (arity, is_schema, variant)? Any client-side `.filter`/`.find`/sort the request could express? Payload columns in a listing path? Paginated with a unique total order? Inside a loop that should be batched?
73	
74	2d. **Contract check.** New/changed shared types: required-vs-optional modeled from real cases (does every producer actually supply it)? Identity carried once (RID) not duplicated decomposed? Consistent with `crossAppContracts.ts` and with what the Obsidian side already assumes — check its consumer code, don't assume.
75	
76	2e. **Converter matrix.** A field added or renamed on a cross-app contract or schema type must be handled in EVERY converter, BOTH directions, or explicitly deferred with a ticket named in the PR. Enumerate the cells and mark each handled/deferred: `packages/database/src/lib/crossAppConverters.ts` (CrossApp→db), `packages/database/src/lib/dbToCrossAppConverters.ts` (db→CrossApp), `apps/roam/src/utils/roamToCrossAppConverters.ts`, and Obsidian's parse/produce paths (`importNodes.ts` parsers, publish side). maparent asked for the missing direction on #1316 AND #1317: "This PR is adding a field; it should handle that field in both translation directions."
77	
78	2f. **Flag-gated writes.** For every new DB write path: which user-visible flag or action authorizes it? Sync flag off ⇒ the user expects NO DB communication; a silent maintenance write (backfill, migration) needs explicit call-out in the PR, and its outcome reports to PostHog — never a user toast (#1332).
79	
80	## Step 3 — Frontend pass (only if FRONTEND files changed)
81	
82	Check against the frontend lessons in `engineering-context.md`, mechanically:
83	- grep the diff for `style=`, `class-[`/`-[` arbitrary values, hex colors → Tailwind-scale violations
84	- grep for `window.roamAlphaAPI` legacy paths (sync `.q`, `async.backend`) → current-API violations
85	- settings writes → must go through block-props accessors, preserving the store gate
86	- new UI elements → which flag gates them (including EXISTING flags the new surface must respect, e.g. `autoCanvasRelations` on #1272); user-facing failures → PostHog + toast, not `console.error`
87	- names: every new variable/setter/label states exactly what it holds or does; UI labels reuse existing product vocabulary ("discourse context", not an invented synonym — #1255)
88	- grep the diff for positional child access on settings/config trees (`tree[3]`, `.children[0]`) → look up by key with `getSubTree`; position compiles today and silently writes to the wrong parent after any reorder (#1302)
89	- persisted/saved data stores stable IDs (shape id, uid), never display names — names are UI-only and subject to change (#1222: save `frameShapeId`, not `frameName`)
90	- `Page`, `Block`, and `Any` are reserved built-in vocabulary: excluded from user-selectable type lists (#1298), never name-resolved to/from a remote schema, never creatable as configured types (#1331 was blocked on exactly this; #1272 applied the same rule on canvas)
91	- a panel that replaces or extends existing UI matches it pixel-wise — proportions, selected-tab highlight, centering; reviewers screenshot-compare against the original (#1255, #1272). Empty states key on the right condition (no relation *instances* ≠ no relation *types*, #1255)
92	- user-facing strings use user vocabulary — a toast saying "backfilled" is a finding; internal bookkeeping reports to PostHog only (#1332)
93	
94	## Step 4 — Process gate
95	
96	- Every hunk maps to this PR's ticket; unrelated changes → revert or explicitly annotate. Out-of-scope improvements a reviewer might request → pre-empt by naming them in the PR with a Linear ticket ("X is deferred to ENG-YYYY").
97	- **One problem, ~<500 lines.** A PR solves a single problem in under ~500 changed lines before tests (mdroidian's stated bar, #1222). Real drive-by bug fixes split into their own ticket — and get fixed at their source layer (a roamjs-components bug is fixed in roamjs-components, not patched locally).
98	- **Bot-comment gate.** Before requesting human review: every codex/graphite/devin comment is either fixed or answered with why-not, and resolved. mdroidian's first pass is frequently just "See codex comments" / "address the bot reviews … and click resolve" (#1257, #1309, #1320) — an unresolved bot thread costs a full review round-trip.
99	- **Chain coverage.** For a PR in a stacked or sibling-ticket chain: does the union of this PR + named sibling tickets cover both platforms and both data directions? "This only handles Obsidian-origin — where's Roam-origin?" is maparent's most repeated 07–08 comment (#1267, #1269, #1316). Name the gap and the ticket that owns it in the PR before he does.
100	- **Guard removals are argued in the PR.** Removing an existence check or gate: state the cases it protected and why each is now safe (idempotent re-upsert, upstream guarantee). #1280's check removal survived review, but through a 3-comment thread that one PR annotation would have preempted.
101	- **Refactor/extraction parity table.** If this PR moves or extracts code (util → shared package, file split, API swap): produce a table of old symbol → new symbol → `identical` or `changed: <why>`. Every not-1:1 replacement is a decision the reviewer WILL ask about ("could you walk through those decisions?") — enumerate them before they do. The table goes in the PR description.
102	- Runtime proof: does this change have a surface a unit test can't exercise (UI, load-order, multi-user)? If yes, a demo is REQUIRED, not noted (`/demo-handoff`). If the diff touches DOM observers, drag/hover interactions, or rendered Roam surfaces: emit a **regression matrix** — surfaces (main window, right sidebar, left sidebar, Kanban, query-builder link/embed/render views, canvas) × content shapes (single-line, multiline/wrapping, nested references, page titles) — marking which cells this change can affect; the demo must drive every affected cell, with the mouse cursor visible in the recording, and any bug you claim fixed must be re-driven by you after the fix. Video quality bar (#1298): signal each state change visually (a quick caption/toast — "before fix" / "on branch"), don't carry it in narration alone, and cut narration that states the obvious ("every relation has a source and destination" earned a 🙄 from mdroidian).
103	- Reviewer context: list the bullets the PR description must contain (what was removed and why, temporary code, decisions made, deferrals + tickets). Test: could someone review this without asking a question?
104	- **Inherited decisions carry breadcrumbs.** Any code that exists because of a review decision on a PREVIOUS PR (a reviewer's direction, a contract agreed in another thread) gets a draft line-comment citing that source ("per maparent on #1214: local IDs may already be RIDs"). Without the breadcrumb the next reviewer re-litigates it.
105	
106	## Output
107	
108	1. **Findings**, ranked by severity, each: file:line — what — why it matters (cite the context-doc entry or the verification step that failed) — concrete fix.
109	2. **Verification log** — one line per mechanical step: what you ran/checked and the outcome. This proves the steps happened; a review with findings but no log is invalid.
110	2b. **Draft PR annotations** — ready-to-post, line-anchored comments explaining every non-obvious decision (guidepost style: what this block does and why, inherited-decision citations, parity-table deltas). Proven repeatedly: #1214, and in 07–08 reviewers replied to annotations in-thread and accepted the argument (#1280 "I accept this argument. Approving.", #1331). Also annotate every LARGE removal or moved block ("this was refactored into abc.ts") — mdroidian asked for exactly this on #1320. Posting them is part of finishing the PR, not optional polish.
111	2c. All reviewer-facing prose this skill emits — PR description bullets, draft annotations, deferral notes, parity tables — follows the team writing style skill at `<repo-root>/.claude/skills/discourse-engineering-writing-style/SKILL.md` (mdroidian's #1278): lead with the point, one term per concept, replace vague verbs ("handle", "support") with the specific behavior, no em dashes, shortest version that keeps the nuance.
112	3. **Predicted review** (simulation, not identity): given the reviewers' comment history — mdroidian: frontend craftsmanship, dead code, reuse, naming, comment noise, bare `!`, second lookups, design parity with existing UI, reserved vocabulary (Page/Block/Any), unresolved bot comments, demo-video quality, Socratic "why is this here?"; maparent: schema/contract correctness, query shape, the missing converter direction, chain/sibling-ticket coverage gaps ("this only handles Obsidian-origin"), values re-fetched that the pipeline already carries, partial-failure semantics, Obsidian-parity of UX decisions, "worth calling out in another task?", "what does the data look like in 6 months?" — list the comments each would most likely leave on the remaining diff. These are forecasts to fix or preempt in the PR description, not instructions to please anyone.
113	4. If a pass is clean, say so explicitly. Do not manufacture findings; ~11% of historical review comments were not catchable pre-PR (product/1:1 context) — surface open questions instead of contorting.
114	
115	Anti-weasel rules: no "not harmful, just unnecessary" (unnecessary = delete), no "acceptable for consistency" (a no-op kept for symmetry is cargo-culting), no noting facts without stating the conclusion they imply. If you have the information that leads to a finding, state the finding.
116	</skill-prompt>
